newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-UNITED THE TEAM TO BEAT AS SEASON STARTS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UNITED THE TEAM TO BEAT AS SEASON STARTS.

text.p: Despite the tens of millions of pounds spent on new players by their rivals during the summer, Manchester United remain clear favourites to win the English League title again this season.

They may have it tougher trying to win it this time, with Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea all set to mount realistic and sustained challenges and Aston Villa, Leeds and Newcastle probably in the hunt too.

But it would be no surprise if United finished clear of the field for the fifth time in six seasons next May even though manager Alex Ferguson has been relatively quiet in the summer transfer market with just one significant signing, the 3.5 million pounds ($5.7 million) acquisition of Teddy Sheringham from Tottenham.
The 31-year-old England forward has been bought as a straight replacement for Eric Cantona, who along with Alan Shearer will be the most significant absentee when the season kicks off this weekend.
The absence of Cantona, who retired at the end of last season, is unlikely to have as much impact at Old Trafford as Shearer's absence will have at St James' Park.
And that is why Newcastle could well find themselves lagging behind in the title race after looking set to be closely involved.

While Sheringham and the emerging Paul Scholes should provide plenty of the attacking creativity conjured up by Cantona, Shearer's absence has considerably weakened Newcastle, who, until two weeks ago looked set to build on their storming second-placed finish last season which earned them a place in the expanded Champions League.

Kenny Dalglish, who acquired England veteran Stuart Pearce from Nottingham Forest on a free transfer and exciting foreigners Temur Ketsbaia of Georgia and Dane Jon Dahl Tomasson, appeared to have shaped a balanced squad ideally placed to bring the title back to Newcastle for the first time since 1927.

But all that changed on the last weekend of July when Shearer fractured his fibula and ruptured his ankle ligaments in the last minute of a meaningless friendly against Chelsea and Newcastle sold his England strike partner Les Ferdinand to Tottenham for 6.0 million pounds ($9.7 million).
In 24 hours the partnership that provided the bulk of Newcastle's goals for the last two seasons was broken.
With Shearer out for possibly most of the season -- damaging not only Newcastle's title hopes but England's World Cup aspirations -- Newcastle could struggle to score enough goals.
That is unlikely to be the trouble at Liverpool, Arsenal or Chelsea who have all significantly strengthened their teams this summer.
It was argued for much of last season that all Liverpool needed to win the title was a player like Paul Ince, so this summer they bought him from Internazionale Milan for 4.2 million pounds.

Ince will add some much needed steel and no little creativity to the Liverpool midfield, but there is no natural centre-half in the backline and Liverpool could again be more let down by defensive frailities than any failings up front.

Manager Roy Evans sold Stan Collymore to Aston Villa for 7.0 million pounds and has replaced him with the German international Karlheinz Riedle from Borussia Dortmund to partner Robbie Fowler in attack.
It's a gamble that must pay off for Evans. If he is to stay with the club he has served for the last 30 years he must bring the title back to Anfield for the first time since 1990.

During the last century Arsenal have been the only side from London to consistently challenge for the title. They are still the capital's most likely contenders, but there was little cockney rhyming slang being heard on the training ground this summer.

French manager Arsene Wenger spent nearly 15.0 million pounds ($24.4 million) on a summer spending spree to secure Frenchmen Emmanuel Petit and Gilles Grimandi, Dutchman Marc Overmars and Portugal's Luis Boa Morte to add to the already large overseas corps at Highbury.

In little over a year Wenger has transformed the way the Gunners play and their newly-found exuberance, coupled with their traditional defensive strengths, could carry them all the way to the title -- or very close.

If Arsenal tighten up their poor disciplinary record and if Ian Wright keeps on scoring -- he is only eight goals away from becoming the club's all-time record scorer -- the title could well be going back to London for the first time since 1991.

Chelsea will be hoping if it does, it will be heading west for the first time since 1955 -- the only time they have been champions. Chelsea manager Ruud Gullit's approach to the transfer market was similiar to Wenger's -- buy the best overseas players at the cheapest prices.

Gullit, who has also registered himself as a player for another season, brought Chelsea some long-overdue success with victory in the F.A. Cup Final in May and signings such as the Uruguayan midfielder Gustavo Poyet, Dutch goalkeeper Ed de Goey and the Nigerian Celestine Babayaro all look set to strengthen what was a promising team to begin with.
Villa -- with Collymore back at the team he supported as a boy in the Midlands -- and Leeds could also feature in the title race.
For others such as Tottenham, Blackburn, Sheffield Wednesday, Wimbledon and Leicester, hope will spring eternal and ambition will probably focus on entry into the UEFA Cup or a good F.A. Cup run.

Barnsley compete in the top flight for the first time in their long history and success for them and their young enterprising manager Danny Wilson would mean a mid-table position and avoiding relegation.
With season ticket and replica kit sales booming, more soccer on television and new grounds at Derby County and first division Sunderland, soccer in England continues to go from strength to strength.
Saturday sees the start of almost 11 months of soccer, and England, despite Shearer's absence, should qualify for the 1998 World Cup which will dominate the headlines almost as much as the league.
